prompt: `a = [1, 2, 3]` then `b = a` then `b.append(4)`. What is `a`?
hint: Ask whether the second line copied anything at all.

choices.text: An error, because a list cannot be shared by two names
choices.why: Sharing is the normal case and is not an error.

choices.text: `[1, 2, 3]`, because `b` got its own copy of the list
choices.why: Assignment binds a second name; it does not copy the value.

choices.text: `[1, 2, 3]`, because `append` returns a new list
choices.why: `append` changes the list in place and returns `None`.
Right — both names refer to the same list, and one of them changed it.

prompt: `x = 5` and then `x = "five"`. What happened?
hint: Values have types; names do not.

choices.text: The name now refers to a string instead of a number
choices.why: Right — Python is dynamically typed, so a name is free to move.

choices.text: The number was converted into the text `"five"` in place
choices.why: Nothing was converted; the second line binds a different value.

choices.text: Both values are kept, and `x` holds the most recent one
choices.why: Only the binding is kept; the 5 is discarded when nothing refers to it.

choices.text: An error, because a name cannot change its type once set
choices.why: It can, which is what dynamic typing means.

prompt: Why is `list = [1, 2]` a mistake even though it runs?

choices.text: It permanently changes `list` for every file in the project

choices.text: It is a keyword, so the interpreter refuses the assignment
choices.why: `list` is a built-in name rather than a keyword, which is why it is allowed.

choices.text: It shadows the built-in, so `list()` cannot be called after it
choices.why: Right — legal, silent, and lesson 17's linter reports exactly this.

prompt: Why is `r"C:\Users\ada"` written with an `r` in front?

choices.text: It marks the string as a file path for the operating system
choices.why: Python attaches no meaning to the path; `pathlib` is lesson 7's answer.

choices.text: It allows the string to contain both kinds of quote
choices.why: Any string can, with the right outer quote or an escape.

choices.text: It makes the string read-only, unlike an ordinary one
choices.why: Every string is already immutable.

choices.text: It turns escape sequences off, so the backslashes stay literal
choices.why: Right — which is why every regular expression in lesson 10 is written this way.

prompt: Why is an f-string the wrong way to build a SQL query?

choices.text: The database receives the string before the values are substituted
choices.why: It receives the finished string, which is precisely why this is unsafe.

choices.text: SQL keywords are reserved inside an f-string and raise
